sourceFacts: Assessment of suspected late-onset neonatal sepsis particularly includes consideration of lumbar puncture and meningitis.
CSF assessment can identify CNS infection; LP safety must be assessed, and urgent antibiotics must not be delayed in a seriously unwell child.
prompt:
Create an entirely original medical teaching concept illustration, landscape 3:2, warm hand-painted watercolour and gouache on ivory paper, fine ink contours, restrained navy labels, muted teal, ochre and peach accents, generous whitespace. Gentle storybook warmth with the precision and legibility of an educational atlas. Use written instructions only; no image reference. Meaningful visual relationships and sparse short labels, not paragraphs in boxes. NO internal anatomy, organ/eye/ear/brain/tissue cutaways, anatomical pathways, bones, diagnostic images, fake scans, realistic lesions, photorealistic skin, glossy wet flesh or 3D tissue. Neutral symbols or fully clothed surface poses only where specified. Preserve every direction, relationship and count in the explicit structure. Title and labels exactly as requested, no additional prose. Footer 'Educational schematic'. No logo or watermark.

Title 'Late-onset neonatal sepsis'. A branching evaluation concept with a small fully wrapped sleeping-infant pictogram at LEFT above caption 'Think beyond the bloodstream'. Two parallel large branches go RIGHT. TOP branch ends at a small closed specimen tube with muted red fluid labelled 'Blood assessment'. LOWER branch goes to a large question-mark token labelled 'Consider meningitis', then to a second closed specimen tube with CLEAR pale-blue fluid labelled 'CSF assessment when safe'. No brain, spinal cord, meninges, body compartments, needle placement, microbes or lab microscope view. The tubes are specimen symbols, not diagnostic appearance. Bottom bold short line 'Urgent treatment must not wait'. No claim all late sepsis has meningitis or that early sepsis excludes it.
